prompt: Perform a cloud IAM review of organization/account roles, federation, workload identities, trust policies, resource policies, KMS grants, wildcard permissions, and cross-account access.
Review cloud posture for a GCP hierarchy using Workload Identity Federation, service accounts, IAM conditions, public storage/serverless exposure, organization policy, and centralized audit logs.
Assess Azure cloud security for Entra identities, managed identities, RBAC scope, public endpoints/private links, Key Vault resource access, diagnostic settings, and policy guardrails.
Design cloud network security with explicit public ingress, private app/data paths, management access, egress destinations, shared-service connectivity, and effective route/resource verification.
Harden a cross-account data path so producer, consumer, resource policy, and KMS permissions are narrowly scoped and all IAM/resource changes are centrally auditable.
Harden Kubernetes container runtime privilege, seccomp, capabilities, host mounts, service accounts, and namespace NetworkPolicy; provider IAM is unchanged.
Define application tenant/object/field/action permissions after the workload has already received its least-privileged cloud identity.
Design the cryptographic key hierarchy, cryptoperiod, envelope wrapping, rotation, revocation, backup, and destruction lifecycle independently of cloud IAM posture.
Verify dependency locks, SLSA provenance, SBOMs, CI builder identity, and artifact signatures before the deployment stage.
Execute the already-defined cloud IAM/public exposure/logging tests and issue the final security verdict; do not redesign cloud policy.
The EKS workload needs cloud security for AWS account/IAM/KMS/resource policy and infrastructure security for pod privilege/mounts/network policy. Keep those provider and runtime layers separate.

The application has user authorization and cloud workload IAM. Keep tenant/resource policy in authorization-security while cloud-security owns provider identity, assume-role trust, and resource permissions.
Cloud resources use KMS encryption. Cloud-security owns which principals/services may access the provider resources and keys; secrets-key-management owns the key hierarchy and lifecycle.
A historical cloud review is attached. Only fix its formatting; do not inspect or change any provider account or policy.
An old permission incident mentions an IAM role. Extract the dates and owners only; no current cloud or application access work is requested.
A KMS README includes a cloud example. Rename one documentation heading only and leave all key and provider behavior unchanged.
